questions.question: In supervised learning, what does the model receive during training?
options: Only input data with no labels, so the model must discover structure entirely on its own
A reward signal for each action taken, which the model uses to adjust its behavior over time
Input-output pairs where the correct answer is provided for each example
A set of if-then rules written by a human expert that the model simply executes
questions.explanation: Supervised learning trains on input-output pairs (labeled data). The model learns to map inputs to known correct outputs.

questions.question: What is the purpose of splitting data into training and test sets?
options: To make training run faster, since the model only has to process the smaller training portion
To evaluate whether the model generalizes to data it has never seen during training, rather than just memorized
To keep a backup copy of the data in case the training set is corrupted or accidentally lost
To balance the class distribution between the two sets so each has an equal number of examples, with no need to inspect intermediate results or test edge cases
questions.explanation: The test set measures generalization. If you evaluate on training data, you measure memorization, not learning.

questions.question: A model gets 98% accuracy on training data but 55% on test data. What is this an example of?
options: Underfitting: the model is too simple to capture the patterns in either set
Data drift: the statistical distribution of the test set changed sometime after training finished
Overfitting: the model memorized training-set noise instead of learning general patterns
Good generalization: the model learned the true underlying patterns in the data
questions.explanation: A large gap between training accuracy (high) and test accuracy (low) is the hallmark of overfitting. The model memorized the training data.

questions.question: An e-commerce site wants to group customers into segments based on purchase behavior without any predefined labels. Which type of ML is this?
options: Supervised learning (classification), since customers are being sorted into distinct categories, before defining the measurement, acceptance threshold, or rollback path
Unsupervised learning (clustering), since the model finds natural groupings without predefined labels
Supervised learning (regression), since purchase behavior is a continuous numeric signal
Reinforcement learning, since the site adjusts its recommendations based on customer responses
questions.explanation: Finding natural groupings in data without predefined labels is clustering, which is a form of unsupervised learning.

questions.question: Which scenario is NOT a good use case for machine learning?
options: Converting temperatures from Celsius to Fahrenheit, a fixed formula that needs no learned model
Predicting customer churn from historical behavior data across many weakly-correlated signals over time
Detecting fraudulent transactions in a continuous stream of millions of payments in real time
Classifying images of skin lesions as benign or malignant from subtle pixel-level patterns
questions.explanation: Celsius to Fahrenheit is a fixed formula (F = 9/5 * C + 32). Simple, well-defined rules do not need ML. ML adds complexity with no benefit.

questions.question: What is the best completion criterion for What Is Machine Learning?
options: Implement a nearest centroid classifier from scratch and evaluate it against a random baseline
Skip validation and trust the first plausible-looking output
Choose a production framework before defining the core mechanism, with no need to inspect intermediate results or test edge cases
Treat one successful example as proof that every edge case works
questions.explanation: “Implement a nearest centroid classifier from scratch and evaluate it against a random baseline” is one of this lesson’s stated outcomes; the other choices bypass its required reasoning or validation.
